lines.act: ACT ONE — The number that refuses to change
lines.text: Suppose you want the height of a tall tree, and you only have a tape measure.

lines.act: ACT ONE — The number that refuses to change
lines.text: You can't reach the top, but you can walk away from it along the ground. Say, twenty meters.

lines.act: ACT ONE — The number that refuses to change
lines.text: From there you look up at the very top, and you measure the angle: thirty-five degrees.

lines.act: ACT ONE — The number that refuses to change
lines.text: That's a right triangle, and you only know one of its sides. It doesn't look like enough.

lines.act: ACT ONE — The number that refuses to change
lines.text: But now draw the same triangle on paper, small enough to measure. Same angles, so the same shape.

lines.act: ACT ONE — The number that refuses to change
lines.text: Your little triangle is a scale model of the real one, which means its proportions are exactly the same.

lines.act: ACT ONE — The number that refuses to change
lines.text: On paper, the height comes out at about zero point seven of the base.

lines.act: ACT ONE — The number that refuses to change
lines.text: So the real tree is zero point seven of twenty meters. About fourteen meters, and you never left the ground.

lines.act: ACT ONE — The number that refuses to change
lines.text: Here's what just happened, and it's the seed of the whole subject.

lines.act: ACT ONE — The number that refuses to change
lines.text: Fix the angle, and the proportions of a right triangle are fixed too, whatever its size.

lines.act: ACT ONE — The number that refuses to change
lines.text: Double the triangle, and both sides double, so their ratio doesn't move.

lines.act: ACT ONE — The number that refuses to change
lines.text: Every angle comes with its own unchanging numbers, and that is all trigonometry was at the start: a list of those numbers.

lines.act: ACT ONE — The number that refuses to change
lines.text: There are three sides, so there are three ratios worth naming.

lines.act: ACT ONE — The number that refuses to change
lines.text: The side across from our angle, divided by the longest side, is called the sine.

lines.act: ACT ONE — The number that refuses to change
lines.text: The side next to our angle, divided by the longest side, is the cosine.

lines.act: ACT ONE — The number that refuses to change
lines.text: And across divided by next to, the one we just used on the tree, is the tangent.

lines.act: ACT ONE — The number that refuses to change
lines.text: Textbooks call those same sides the opposite, the adjacent and the hypotenuse, and you may have met them as soh cah toa. Same ratios, longer names.

lines.act: ACT ONE — The number that refuses to change
lines.text: Notice what those are not. Sine isn't a length, and it isn't a kind of angle.

lines.act: ACT ONE — The number that refuses to change
lines.text: It's a plain number, a ratio, and it has no units at all.

lines.act: ACT ONE — The number that refuses to change
lines.text: For thirty degrees that number is exactly one half, and we can even see why.

lines.act: ACT ONE — The number that refuses to change
lines.text: Take a triangle with three equal sides, and cut it straight down the middle.

lines.act: ACT ONE — The number that refuses to change
lines.text: The short side is now half of the long side, and the angle across from it is thirty degrees. So the sine of thirty is one half. No memorizing needed.

lines.act: ACT ONE — The number that refuses to change
lines.text: So zero point five was the honest answer. Then where on earth does minus zero point nine eight eight come from?

lines.act: ACT ONE — The number that refuses to change
lines.text: A ratio of two lengths can't even be negative.

lines.act: ACT ONE — The number that refuses to change
lines.text: Something about this definition is too small.

lines.act: ACT TWO — One point on a circle
lines.text: Try the sine of one hundred and twenty degrees.

lines.act: ACT TWO — One point on a circle
lines.text: A right triangle already spends ninety degrees on its corner, so the other two angles have to share what's left. One hundred and twenty simply doesn't fit.

lines.act: ACT TWO — One point on a circle
lines.text: By our definition, the question has no answer. And yet the calculator says zero point eight six six, without hesitating.

lines.act: ACT TWO — One point on a circle
lines.text: So the calculator must know a better definition than the one we just learned.

lines.act: ACT TWO — One point on a circle
lines.text: Here it is, and it starts with a small trick.

lines.act: ACT TWO — One point on a circle
lines.text: Take our triangle and make the longest side exactly one.

lines.act: ACT TWO — One point on a circle
lines.text: Now dividing by the longest side does nothing, so the sine is simply the height of the triangle, and the cosine is simply its width.

lines.act: ACT TWO — One point on a circle
lines.text: Next, stand that triangle at the center of a circle of radius one.

lines.act: ACT TWO — One point on a circle
lines.text: Its tip sits on the rim. Call that tip M.

lines.act: ACT TWO — One point on a circle
lines.text: As the angle opens, M slides along the rim, and the triangle's width and height just follow it.

lines.act: ACT TWO — One point on a circle
lines.text: So the cosine is how far M is across, and the sine is how far M is up.

lines.act: ACT TWO — One point on a circle
lines.text: That's the better definition. Cosine and sine are the two coordinates of one point on a circle.

lines.act: ACT TWO — One point on a circle
lines.text: For angles a triangle can hold, it gives exactly the same numbers as before, so nothing we learned was wrong.

lines.act: ACT TWO — One point on a circle
lines.text: It just doesn't stop at ninety degrees.

lines.act: ACT TWO — One point on a circle
lines.text: Keep opening the angle to one hundred and twenty degrees.

lines.act: ACT TWO — One point on a circle
lines.text: There's no triangle to worry about now, only a point that has kept walking.

lines.act: ACT TWO — One point on a circle
lines.text: M is still high up, so its height is zero point eight six six, the number the calculator gave us.

lines.act: ACT TWO — One point on a circle
lines.text: That's the same height it had at sixty degrees, on the other side. Remember that, it comes back next time.

lines.act: ACT TWO — One point on a circle
lines.text: But look at M's across coordinate. M has crossed to the left of center, so its cosine is minus one half.

lines.act: ACT TWO — One point on a circle
lines.text: And there's our first negative number. A side of a triangle can't be negative, but a coordinate can.

lines.act: ACT TWO — One point on a circle
lines.text: Which means you never have to memorize the signs.

lines.act: ACT TWO — One point on a circle
lines.text: Is M on the left? Then the cosine is negative. Is M below the center? Then the sine is negative.

lines.act: ACT TWO — One point on a circle
lines.text: That's the entire table of signs, and you can see it from across the room.

lines.section: What the picture gives you for free
lines.act: ACT TWO — One point on a circle
lines.text: M lives on a circle of radius one, so its across and its up form a right triangle with a long side of one.

lines.section: What the picture gives you for free
lines.act: ACT TWO — One point on a circle
lines.text: Pythagoras says that across squared, plus up squared, equals one.

lines.section: What the picture gives you for free
lines.act: ACT TWO — One point on a circle
lines.text: Written in our new words, that's sine squared plus cosine squared equals one, for every angle there is.

lines.section: What the picture gives you for free
lines.act: ACT TWO — One point on a circle
lines.text: This is the most used identity in trigonometry, and it's nothing more than the statement that M is on the circle.

lines.section: What the picture gives you for free
lines.act: ACT TWO — One point on a circle
lines.text: And the famous angles can now be read right off the circle.

lines.section: What the picture gives you for free
lines.act: ACT TWO — One point on a circle
lines.text: At thirty degrees, M is one half up. At sixty, across and up simply trade places, so M is zero point eight six six up and one half across.

lines.section: What the picture gives you for free
lines.act: ACT TWO — One point on a circle
lines.text: At forty-five, across and up are equal, and their squares add to one, so each is root two over two. About zero point seven zero seven.

lines.section: What the picture gives you for free
lines.act: ACT TWO — One point on a circle
lines.text: Tangent gets a picture as well. It's up divided by across, and that is exactly the slope of the line from the center to M.

lines.section: What the picture gives you for free
lines.act: ACT TWO — One point on a circle
lines.text: At ninety degrees, that line stands straight up. Its slope doesn't exist, and neither does the tangent of ninety degrees.

lines.section: What the picture gives you for free
lines.act: ACT TWO — One point on a circle
lines.text: Nothing has gone wrong there. Your calculator's error message is telling the truth.

lines.section: What the picture gives you for free
lines.act: ACT TWO — One point on a circle
lines.text: So we know what sine really measures now: height on a circle.

lines.section: What the picture gives you for free
lines.act: ACT TWO — One point on a circle
lines.text: But the height at thirty is one half, and the calculator also said minus zero point nine eight eight.

lines.section: What the picture gives you for free
lines.act: ACT TWO — One point on a circle
lines.text: For that, we have to ask what the word thirty actually meant.

lines.act: ACT THREE — What thirty means
lines.text: Degrees cut a full turn into three hundred and sixty parts.

lines.act: ACT THREE — What thirty means
lines.text: It's a handy number, but nothing about a circle asks for it. Someone had to choose it.

lines.act: ACT THREE — What thirty means
lines.text: Here's a way to measure an angle with no choices at all.

lines.act: ACT THREE — What thirty means
lines.text: Start at the right of the circle, and walk along the rim until you've walked exactly one radius.

lines.act: ACT THREE — What thirty means
lines.text: The angle you've swept out is called one radian. It's a little over fifty-seven degrees.

lines.act: ACT THREE — What thirty means
lines.text: It's the same on any circle, a coin or the whole Earth, since it only compares the rim with that circle's own radius.

lines.act: ACT THREE — What thirty means
lines.text: So how many radians are in a full turn? The rim is two pi times the radius, so a full turn is two pi radians. About six point two eight.

lines.act: ACT THREE — What thirty means
lines.text: Half a turn is pi, and a quarter turn is pi over two.

lines.act: ACT THREE — What thirty means
lines.text: So one hundred and eighty degrees is pi, and that's the only conversion you need. Thirty degrees is a sixth of that, so pi over six.

lines.act: ACT THREE — What thirty means
lines.text: This is why mathematicians love radians. On a circle of any size, the arc you walk is just the angle times the radius, with no extra factor.

lines.act: ACT THREE — What thirty means
lines.text: And since this is just distance along the rim, on a circle of radius one, an angle in radians is simply how far M has walked.

lines.act: ACT THREE — What thirty means
lines.text: Now we can finally go back to our calculator.

lines.act: ACT THREE — What thirty means
lines.text: In degree mode, thirty means a twelfth of a turn, and M's height is one half.

lines.act: ACT THREE — What thirty means
lines.text: That one setting we changed switches it to radians, and now thirty means this: walk thirty units along the rim.

lines.act: ACT THREE — What thirty means
lines.text: So let's walk. Each full turn takes about six point two eight.

lines.act: ACT THREE — What thirty means
lines.text: Four turns use up just over twenty-five. And after each whole turn, M stands exactly where it started, so all of those turns change nothing.

lines.act: ACT THREE — What thirty means
lines.text: That's what we mean when we say sine repeats, and it's the last piece.

lines.act: ACT THREE — What thirty means
lines.text: We have about four point eight seven left to walk.

lines.act: ACT THREE — What thirty means
lines.text: That carries M past the left side, past the bottom, and stops it nearly two hundred and seventy-nine degrees around, low on the right.

lines.act: ACT THREE — What thirty means
lines.text: Almost at the very bottom of the circle.

lines.act: ACT THREE — What thirty means
lines.text: Its height there is minus zero point nine eight eight.

lines.act: ACT THREE — What thirty means
lines.text: Same keys, and two different points on the same circle.

lines.act: ACT THREE — What thirty means
lines.text: The calculator was never confused. We just never told it how far to walk.

lines.act: ACT THREE — What thirty means
lines.text: So before you trust a sine on a calculator, check that little setting.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — Putting it together
lines.text: An angle fixes the proportions of a right triangle, and those proportions are sine, cosine and tangent.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — Putting it together
lines.text: Put the triangle in a circle of radius one, and cosine and sine become the coordinates of a point, which can go anywhere, and can go negative.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — Putting it together
lines.text: And radians measure the walk itself, so going around again changes nothing, and thirty units lands you near the bottom.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — Putting it together
lines.text: Here's something to try before the next video. Find a second angle whose sine is exactly one half.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — Putting it together
lines.text: You won't need a calculator. Just look for another point on the circle at the same height.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — Putting it together
lines.text: Next time we'll use that same trick to turn a whole page of formulas you were told to memorize into four simple pictures.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — Putting it together
lines.text: And later in the series, we'll keep M walking and write down its height as it goes, and the circle will unroll into a wave.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — Putting it together
lines.text: This is the first part of our trigonometry series on 99% from scratch. Thanks for watching, and I'll see you in the next one.
